Vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was thirty-two when he was mugged outside a subway station in the financial district where he had ducked in to use the bathroom before his evening commute home. Two men approached from behind a column—he had not seen them until they were already moving toward him. One grabbed his arm while the other shoved him against the tiled wall. The impact knocked the wind from his lungs. They took his wallet, his phone, his watch. What stayed with him most vividly was not the force of the shove but the smell of stale cigarette smoke mixed with something chemical, and the taste of blood from where his lip split against his teeth. One of the men had leaned close to his ear and said something low and fast that Marcus could not fully process in the moment. The whole thing lasted perhaps ninety seconds. A transit officer found him sitting on the floor a few minutes later, shaking.

Six years have passed since then, and Marcus has built a life that appears, from the outside, largely intact. He married Sarah three years ago. He teaches high school history at a public school in a stable neighborhood. He maintains friendships, pays his mortgage, shows up to faculty meetings. But the texture of his daily existence has become increasingly constrained, and in the past year the constraints have begun to visibly affect his work and his marriage.

Marcus has come to understand the world as fundamentally unpredictable and hostile in ways he cannot quite articulate to others. Faces have become a source of constant vigilance. When he stands before his class—a room of teenagers he intellectually knows pose no threat—his eyes move across their expressions searching for signs of aggression, calculation, the micro-expressions he has convinced himself reveal true intent. He finds himself studying the set of a student's jaw, the intensity of their gaze, wondering if something dangerous is being concealed. This hypervigilance has exhausted him. Colleagues have noticed that he seems tense, that he sometimes appears startled by ordinary classroom sounds—a door slamming, a desk scraping—and recoils as if struck. One student asked, in the direct way teenagers do, why he always looked scared.

Crowded spaces have become nearly intolerable. The subway is out of the question; Marcus drives to school now, though driving itself has become complicated. He cannot tolerate passengers. When Sarah suggests they take a trip together, or when a colleague asks for a ride to a conference, Marcus finds himself inventing reasons why this is impossible. Last month, when Sarah's sister visited from out of state and needed a ride from the airport, Marcus's anxiety was so acute that he had to pull over twice. Sarah had to take over driving. The silence in the car afterward felt accusatory, though she said nothing. He knows she does not understand why he cannot simply manage this, why he cannot sit in a car with another person without his heart rate climbing and his palms becoming slick.

Movie theaters are impossible. Shopping malls are impossible. The crowded hallways between classes at school have become a gauntlet he dreads. He times his movement through them carefully, positioning himself against walls, always aware of where the nearest exit is located. The moment he enters any enclosed space—a classroom, a staff room, a restaurant—his attention fractures. Part of him is present in conversation; another part is mapping the room's geometry, identifying windows, doors, alternative routes. He is exhausted by this constant spatial calculation, yet the moment he stops doing it, panic rises.

The memories themselves come without warning and with a sensory completeness that unmoors him from the present. He will be standing at the front of his classroom explaining the causes of the Civil War, and suddenly he tastes blood again, smells that chemical smoke, feels the impact of the wall against his spine. The memory does not feel like remembering—it feels like the event is happening now, all of it at once, pressing in from every direction. These episodes last seconds or minutes, but they leave him shaken, disoriented. His students have learned not to ask questions when he goes quiet mid-sentence.

What troubles Marcus most deeply is the conviction that this happened because the world is simply dangerous, that he was unlucky, and that no real justice has been possible. The police never found the men. The case went nowhere. He has come to believe that institutions—the police, the legal system—fundamentally failed him, and that this failure is not exceptional but revealing. It showed him something true about how the world actually works. This belief sits beneath everything else, a bedrock conviction that shapes how he moves through his days.

Sarah suggested, gently and then less gently, that he see someone. She said she loved him but that she was frightened by how much space the fear was taking up in their life together. Marcus finally called a therapist last week. He is afraid of what it will mean if the fear cannot be fixed, and hopeful, in a way he has not allowed himself to be in years, that someone might help him understand why his mind has decided the world is a place where he cannot be safe.
